title: Range Types & Overlap Operators
description: Model temporal spans and numeric ranges using TSRANGE, DATERANGE, INT4RANGE, and the overlap operator &&.

data.text: In traditional databases, modeling a date range requires two separate columns (`start_date` and `end_date`) and complex `WHERE (start1 <= end2 AND end1 >= start2)` logic. PostgreSQL includes built-in **Range Types** (`DATERANGE`, `TSRANGE`, `TSTZRANGE`, `NUMRANGE`) that represent contiguous ranges of values.

data.title: Hotel Booking Overlap Check with && Operator
data.content: Using the overlap operator && to detect conflicting room reservations.

data.text: A range literal is written `[lower, upper)`. Square brackets include the bound; parentheses exclude it. The default is `[)`, and it is the convention that avoids double-counting: an event from Monday 00:00 to Tuesday 00:00 and the next from Tuesday 00:00 do not overlap because the boundary belongs to exactly one range.

data.title: Constructing and Inspecting Ranges
data.content: `lower_inc` and `upper_inc` make the boundary semantics explicit.
data.code:
SELECT '[2026-01-01, 2026-02-01)'::daterange AS default_bounds,
       '[2026-01-01, 2026-02-01]'::daterange AS closed_bounds,
       daterange('2026-01-01', '2026-02-01', '[)') AS explicit;

SELECT lower(r) AS start, upper(r) AS end,
       lower_inc(r) AS includes_start,
       upper_inc(r) AS includes_end
FROM (SELECT '[2026-01-01, 2026-02-01)'::daterange AS r) s;

-- Unbounded and empty ranges
SELECT daterange('2026-01-01', NULL) AS open_ended,
       daterange(NULL, '2026-12-31') AS from_beginning,
       'empty'::daterange            AS empty_range;

-- Canonical form: [) ranges with no inclusive upper bound
SELECT '[2026-01-01, 2026-02-01]'::daterange;   -- displays as [2026-01-01,2026-02-02)

data.title: Preventing Double Bookings With an Exclusion Constraint
data.content: This is the killer feature: the database guarantees no overlap.
data.code:
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;   -- needed for the room_number equality part

CREATE TABLE room_bookings (
    id          BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    room_number INT NOT NULL,
    stay        DATERANGE NOT NULL,
    -- No two rows may have the same room with overlapping stays
    CONSTRAINT no_overlap
        EXCLUDE USING gist (room_number WITH =, stay WITH &&),
    CONSTRAINT stay_valid CHECK (NOT isempty(stay))
);

INSERT INTO room_bookings (room_number, stay)
VALUES (101, daterange('2026-12-24','2026-12-28'));

INSERT INTO room_bookings (room_number, stay)
VALUES (101, daterange('2026-12-27','2026-12-30'));
-- ERROR: conflicting key value violates exclusion constraint "no_overlap"

-- Bookings that overlap Christmas week
SELECT * FROM room_bookings
WHERE stay && daterange('2026-12-24','2026-12-31');

data.text: Note that the exclusion constraint needs a GiST index, and mixing an equality column with a range needs the `btree_gist` extension. That combination — `EXCLUDE USING gist (key WITH =, period WITH &&)` — is the standard way to enforce non-overlap for bookings, pricing tiers, and employment periods.

data.title: Interview Answer
data.text: When asked "how do you prevent overlapping date ranges without application locks?", answer: a GiST **exclusion constraint** over `(key WITH =, period WITH &&)`. It is enforced inside the database, so it holds even under concurrent inserts.

steps: Add an exclusion constraint so one product cannot have overlapping tiers.

data.expectedOutcome: A table whose integrity is guaranteed by the engine, not by hope.

items.question: Should I use a range type or two columns?
items.answer: Use a range type when overlap detection, containment, or adjacency matters — the operators and GiST indexing are worth it. Two columns are fine for simple reporting where you never ask "do these overlap?".

items.question: Why is the default bound `[)`?
items.answer: It makes ranges partitionable: consecutive ranges can share a boundary without overlapping, which is exactly what you want for scheduling and accounting periods.

items.question: How do ranged queries use an index?
items.answer: Create a GiST index on the range column. The planner can use it for `&&`, `@>`, and `<@`; a btree index cannot answer overlap questions.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Range types encapsulate continuous spans with inclusivity markers `[)`, `[]`, etc.
The `&&` operator checks if two ranges overlap.
Range types can be paired with GiST indexes and exclusion constraints to guarantee non-overlapping reservations.
